phrases.english_text: We’re not all like that now, because they get married and bring different people. A white man joined us, and I robbed him. He moved in and his name was Jim Capps. I was watching and as soon as he left, I went in and helped myself. It wasn’t very long, and they caught up to me. And they let us all go. We never bothered him again. But we would throw rocks at him when he drove by. He was the only one who had a car up there, we used to just walk around. Someone was rich if they rode by on a horse. Boy, he was lucky I didn’t hit him in the head. Really, they weren’t any good. Of course, I was with them too. It was boss’s older brother; he was the one who started it all. They used to get away with it. We would get the blame for it. The rest of us would get in trouble and they would be laughing. They’re the ones that started it. Those people down Bell, we didn’t get along because we never came down. We just stayed up there in woods with no shoes on. I wonder how thick the soles of our feet were. We would run through the woods like it was nothing. Sometimes you would see someone with a toe ye big [gestures] because they stumped their toe. Where they stumped it somewhere. We didn’t go off the hill until we were older but them older boys on the hill would tell them Bell boys to leave us alone. Sometimes I wondered why and then my grandpa said, “It’s because you boys that grew up the hill don’t act right because y’all didn’t grow up around other people.” I guess we did just live in the woods. That’s what I think anyway. Sometimes my grandpa would ask, “What did you do?” They would say, “Someone did something.” They would all look at me. I’m not that foolish. Yeah, I make a lot of mistakes, but not that Bad.

phrases.english_text: We’re not all like that now, because they get married and bring different people. A white man joined us, and I robbed him. He moved in and his name was Jim Capps. I was watching and as soon as he left, I went in and helped myself. It wasn’t very long, and they caught up to me. And they let us all go. We never bothered him again. But we would throw rocks at him when he drove by. He was the only one who had a car up there, we used to just walk around. Someone was rich if they rode by on a horse. Boy, he was lucky I didn’t hit him in the head. Really, they weren’t any good. Of course, I was with them too. It was boss’s older brother; he was the one who started it all. They used to get away with it. We would get the blame for it. The rest of us would get in trouble and they would be laughing. They’re the ones that started it. Those people down Bell, we didn’t get along because we never came down. We just stayed up there in woods with no shoes on. I wonder how thick the soles of our feet were. We would run through the woods like it was nothing. Sometimes you would see someone with a toe ye big [gestures] because they stumped their toe. Where they stumped it somewhere. We didn’t go off the hill until we were older but them older boys on the hill would tell them Bell boys to leave us alone. Sometimes I wondered why and then my grandpa said, “It’s because you boys that grew up the hill don’t act right because y’all didn’t grow up around other people.” I guess we did just live in the woods. That’s what I think anyway. Sometimes my grandpa would ask, “What did you do?” They would say, “Someone did something.” They would all look at me. I’m not that foolish. Yeah, I make a lot of mistakes, but not that Bad.

phrases.english_text: Yeah, it wasn’t till then. It wasn’t until I started school at Greasy, I began to understand English a little bit. I was sixth grade when I started understanding English, but it was still Cherokee on the mountain. The school on the mountain, we were scolded for speaking Cherokee. We used to point at the teacher and say, “You speak your language and we’re talking amongst ourselves.” But we really didn’t get a whopping. Even if he did, they couldn’t whoop us because they couldn’t catch us, we were too fast. Do y’all remember Charlie Canoe? He was old man.

phrases.english_text: Squirrel wasn’t human, he really was a squirrel. He was our uncle too. You couldn’t tell him nothing, but he couldn’t tell us nothing either, cause if he did, he’d have been better off talking to that wall because we didn’t listen to him either. All those Teehees came from the mountain, but my grandma was a Step. Julio Step was my grandpa. He was scary, that was my grandpa, my grandma’s brother, and there was another that was my grandma’s sister, and that was Squirrel’s mom, Tsiyvnsdi was her name. Those were the only three that I know of, that were born there, I don’t know where they came from beyond that. My grandma was a Step, but my grandpa, I think his kinfolk were from Vian, cause every now and then I would take him over there, for about a week and then I’d go get him. I never did get to know them well, and he’d say, “Just know these are your kinfolk,” and I’d really be looking around for some women too.

phrases.english_text: I used to, but I broke my finger. I bit too hard on a hamburger. No, I smashed my fingers bad, and I couldn’t play guitar after that. All the time, we used to have guitars where we used to live, and we all gathered in the evenings, and we would sing in Cherokee. There was an old man up there named Columbus Pritchett, my aunt’s husband. He used to teach us and tell us how to behave. Every evening we would sing church songs. And then I would start singing country and western and I would mess everything up and then I’d be all by myself again. But it was good though. But in time people would back away and after a while it was just us. Burt Scraper showed up. Boy he was a good fiddle player. “Where did you learn that?” I asked him. He said, “California, that’s where I’m from.” Man, I really believed him too. He just came out of the ground over there. He was born by Lyon Switch. I found that out one day.

phrases.english_text: There was just five of us. My aunt had about 20 kids. She said, “The Bible says go replenish the earth.” I think it was at Cherry Tree, Jerry Nofire said, his wife said, “Yeah, but it didn’t tell you just to do it by yourself.” And his wife was sitting there, and they had about eight or nine kids themselves. Bull is his son. He was a third-generation preacher at Cherry Tree. But Jerry started getting sick all the time, and we knew he was going to pass soon. He said, “Y’all be thinking about who’s going to be preaching for y’all,” sometime around a year before he passed. I was talking to Bull about how he should be the one [who preaches for us], and he said, “I’ve been asking for that for a long time.” We were talking and I chose Bull, and I said, “If you agree to do so, it would be you.” He said, “Let me think about it.” And then he said, “Yeah I will, because we’re going to lose that old man before too long.” And it wasn’t about a year before he really started to get sick and going in and out of the hospital. One time he came back from the hospital, and he got on to us there at church, he said, “You guys here, you’re always praying for me to get better, it’s your fault I’m still here. I’m actually ready to leave.” He was ready to leave, it was because of us praying for him, we were trying to hang on to him. He was ready to leave, that was how he was seeing it, because his wife had already left. “Well, I can’t do anything, I have to pray for you, because that’s what you’ve been teaching us,” is what I told him. We were doing what he told us to do, but he still didn’t like it because he was wanting to go home. One day he went in, they gave up on him, there wasn’t any need for them to know, and he did go home, and then people began to gather at his house. It was like buzzards when they see something laying there. They were eating, and the old man was still hanging in there. We went to visit him, I was doing something at the church, and there was a little girl that came running over to us, she said, “Somebody wants to talk to you,” and I said, “Hang on a minute, let me finish up.” She said, “He’s sitting right there,” and when I went out, there he was after they had given up on him. We talked for a long time, and I said, “What happened?” and he said, “I didn’t feel like going home, so I just thought I better get up.” He was driving that thing that runs by itself, wheelchair. He came to the church, and he said, “I guess they ate everything up, they gave up and went home.” He lasted for about a week after that, and then we were starting to figure it out, that it was close. I visited him every day until the evening, and then one evening I left, I told him I’d come back tomorrow, but first I had to go to town, and it was about 10pm when I got back, and then the phone rang, and he had left.

phrases.english_text: Yeah, he had taught us good. Those people around Salem will tell us, “You guys on the mountain don’t understand nothing,” but we were following the word that was in the Bible, because adulterers can’t get in there. There’s one in there, but he knows, I told him, “You might be the reason good things aren’t happening.” But that girl knows. It was Jerry’s daughter. She tried to take part in the communion, and she was acting like a Christian, but they wouldn’t let her. They told her. “You can come to church here as much as you want, but you can’t take part in the communion.” And she got mad and left for a long time. She was out of church for a long time, but when Jerry passed, she came back and rededicated. But Bull, something happened. I’m not quite sure what happened, I told Bull I wasn’t going to take part in that kind of work. There’s about three of them that don’t need to be in there, but I can’t do anything about it. But one was from another place, Steve Campbell. He’s no good. His wife used to be married. Her husband is still alive somewhere, and that’s no good. Steve Campbell is a licensed minister, and they did take it away. He was at Four Vision's [Baptist] Church, and he left for a long time, and when he came back, he told them he lied to them. He said they had taken his license away but that didn’t stop him from going around and preaching, and even today he still preaches, but not around here. They don’t let him around here, they said he was preaching at some Holiness church. “A Baptist ain’t got no business at a Holiness church,” I told him. That’s what they used to tell us. If a Baptist was preaching at a Holiness church and if that person believes, he will have to go to a Baptist church, not a Holiness church.

phrases.english_text: It was hard because we all went through that. I was always mad because I didn’t understand and did not know why all the other kids had mothers and I didn’t have one and it made me mad. I didn’t understand why. I was always mad at someone and that’s why I learned how to fight. From that time on I found out how strong God is. One time I was somewhere far away driving and drinking, and I was told to stop, and I stopped in the middle of the road, and I go out and walked back and sat down and looked toward my car. Someone was talking to me, but I knew I was drunk, and I didn’t know what was happening to me. Something had told me to park that car somewhere go home and go to church. Something was talking to me like that. I got back in my car and just sat there until morning. That scared me because someone was talking to me, and I was by myself. I could hear someone talking but I couldn’t see anybody. I changed then and started going to church. I never will go back to where I was at. I’m going forward. It’s been 28 years.

phrases.english_text: It’s not like that anymore. People have scattered away, as far as I can see. Long time ago when someone was sick, that’s where everyone would go and help. They would clean and cook. They would finish cleaning and go cut wood. I would join in on things like that. Sometimes we were there for a few days and then when they got better, we would just scatter away. When someone would pass away, that’s what they would do, too. They would stay a few days until they would bury him. We would follow them all the way to the grave and they would say, “This is as far as we can go.” Then we all scatter away but nowadays they just get together and eat like they’re happy they left.

phrases.english_text: Like you said earlier, did you all up the hill help each other when that would happen?

phrases.english_text: Even if someone was having a hard time we would go and help them out. Or if they were sick or if he needed to buy something to eat, we would all go to the woods and cut posts and make railroad ties. There was one person who had a truck, and they would go get him. His name was Nick Springwater. He had a big truck. He would come and take those, and they would buy food with it. We never got any of that. They would give some of that out especially to the one who was sick. 100 lbs. sack of potatoes wasn’t nothing and they would also give them a bag of beans. They would just put them in plastic bags. Or that would give them flour and things like that. I didn’t know what bologna was back then.

phrases.english_text: I don’t have any grandkids, but I have a lot of nieces and nephews. One boy somewhere. I haven’t seen him since he was a baby. I left a long time ago. She lost it, she lost the baby. I don’t know if she did it on purpose and one day we separated. We got together again and then one day she did have a child, but we had already separated again, and that boy grew up somewhere. I haven’t seen him since he was this [gestures] tall. He's grown now, he's about 40 years old and he lives somewhere. I wouldn’t want to see him; I wonder how ugly he is.
